headline: Effective marginal tax rate of ~65 cents in the dollar on age pensioners earning above a day-and-a-half's minimum wage is discouraging workforce participation and exacerbating labour shortages
reasoning: Davidson explains that age pensioners face a 50-cent benefit clawback for every dollar earned above approximately one-and-a-half days of minimum wage pay, and because combined income including the pension is taxable, the bottom marginal tax bracket is then applied on top of that clawback. The resulting effective marginal tax rate of roughly 65 cents in the dollar makes it financially punishing for pensioners to work, directly reducing labour supply at a time when the economy has persistent vacancies. The same clawback structure applies to students on Youth Allowance.
quote: Age pensioners and the students on the Youth Allowance have this clawback, this rapture clawback for every. So for pensioners, for every dollar that they earn over approximately a day and 1/2 on minimum wage, they get $0.50 taken off their benefits. And because their combined income and their age pension is captured as taxable income, then they get the additional bottom bracket tax rate added on to that $0.50 claw back. So for so age, pensioners as a result face an effective marginal tax rate of roughly $0.65 on the dollar for every for every dollar that they earn over a day and 1/2 on minimum wage, which is which is simply unfair. It's unfair. And also it discourages them from working.
episode_title: The tax trap keeping Australians out of work

headline: Australia's 325,000+ job vacancies have persisted for over five years with no effective government solution, weighing on wages and productivity across the economy
reasoning: Saxon Davidson argues that job vacancies have remained at or above 325,000 for five years and three months, well above the pre-COVID average of 180,000–190,000. He contends the government's elevated migration programme has failed to address the shortfall, with only one net job vacancy filled for every ten net migrants. The mismatch is attributed to migrants lacking the skills required for sectors in shortage, particularly construction and manufacturing. The persistence of the problem at near-full employment amplifies broader productivity consequences for the economy.
quote: Unfortunately, they've been at or above 325,000 people for the last five years and 1/4. And the government has no real solution at the moment to address this. And this comes this has many consequences for the broader economy. First and foremost, it's foregone wages for Australians who are not working or filling these job vacancies. But also there's the broader productivity issues arising from the fact that businesses don't simply don't have the workers that they need to provide goods and services to the broader community.

headline: Construction labour shortage ~20% above pre-pandemic levels, threatening the 1.2 million homes target with not one quarterly milestone met since its announcement
reasoning: Davidson notes that construction labour shortages are approximately 20% higher than in February 2020, ranking among the fourth or fifth worst sectors economy-wide. Manufacturing, also critical to housing supply, is similarly elevated. Since the National Housing Accord target of 1.2 million homes by decade's end was announced, not a single quarterly construction target has been met. He argues the government is not serious about fixing the problem given the absence of a genuine solution to the construction worker shortage.
quote: The shortages in construction are about 20% higher now than what they were in February 2020. And that is maybe the 4th or the 5th highest in all the sectors of the economy. Manufacturing, which is another industry that's key for our housing sector and to meet the housing accord, is also significantly higher than it was in February 2020. Ever since the government announced the National Housing called the 1.2 million homes by the end of the decade. Not if you average out the amount of houses that are needed every financial quarter, not one target, not one of those financial quarter targets have been met.

headline: Record immigration programme failing to fill vacancies: fewer than half of skilled visa arrivals are genuinely skilled, and most lack construction-relevant skills
reasoning: Davidson cites IPA research finding that less than half of people arriving on skilled visas are actually skilled, and those who are skilled are often not in the sectors most needed. The government justified its elevated migration programme by pointing to job vacancies, but for every ten net migrants only one net vacancy was filled, making migration a 'lazy solution' that has not worked during the Albanese government's first term. International students make up a large share of arrivals and are not filling skilled vacancies.
quote: There was recent research by the Institute of Public Affairs that found that less than half of the people that are coming to Australia on the skilled visa programme are actually skilled. And of those people that are skilled, they are often not in sectors of the economy that we need directly... For every 10 net migrants that enter the country, only one net job vacancy was filled. So it's simply not working. And it's turned into sort of a lazy solution in the fact that it is continued to not work.
